title: Python Scope: Same Variable, 3 Different Values
description:
One variable name, three totally different printed values -- and it's not a bug. This Short breaks down Python's LEGB scope rule (Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in) and shows why you need the `global` keyword if you actually want to change an outer variable from inside a function.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-1/04-functions-scope/

#Shorts

beats.narration: Same variable name, three completely different values printed in the same run. This is Python's LEGB scope rule at work.
Local beats enclosing beats global beats built-in. Inside inner, x is local. Back in outer, x is enclosing. Outside everything, x is still global -- untouched.

display.code:
x = "global"

def outer():
    x = "enclosing"

    def inner():
        x = "local"
        print(x)  # local

    inner()
    print(x)  # enclosing

outer()
print(x)  # global

beats.narration: Want to change a global from inside a function instead of shadowing it? You need the global keyword -- say Python: don't create a new local, use the outer one.

display.code:
counter = 0

def increment():
    global counter
    counter += 1

beats.narration: Skip global and increment() just creates a throwaway local variable -- your global counter never moves.

display.heading: No `global`? No update.
display.subheading: counter += 1 silently creates a new local variable instead

beats.narration: Scope rules like this are exactly why your variables sometimes 'don't update' -- go see the full breakdown in the lesson.
